intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("a periodic" → aperiodic, "cannard / cannab" → canard, "after of / off / ARC CG" → aft of / aft CG, "retrum" → retrim, "neutally" → neutrally, "fugoid" → phugoid, "PO" → PIO, "gustors / yores / yoring" → gust yaws / yaws / yawing, "your / y" → yaw, "sides slip / sid slip / sidel / sidelit" → sideslip, "dihagal" → dihedral, "vententral" → ventral, "Nassels / nasels" → nacelles, "propw wash" → propwash, "go-ound" → go-around, "Dutch role" → Dutch roll, "gloing / gforces" → g-loading / g-forces, "weather veins" → weathercocks, "queue" → cue; the closing "Standing down" is noise). Before teaching: (1) page 1 — the cover reads "081 08 01 04 - Straight Steady Glide"; correct it to 081 04 01 00 Static and Dynamic Stability; page 2 uses a cropped third-party image with a "pilotmall.com" watermark — replace; (2) page 6 — the restoring moments are reversed on the slide: an AoA INCREASE (nose up) must give a NOSE-DOWN restoring moment, and a decrease a NOSE-UP moment (the recording is correct); (3) page 9 — "AFT CG: negative static stability, tends to diverge" is wrong inside the CG limits: an aft CG gives REDUCED positive stability; it becomes neutral only at the neutral point and negative aft of it. The elevator-effectiveness boxes are also reversed: forward CG → heavier stick forces and the elevator may run out of authority in the flare; aft CG → lighter, more sensitive elevator, smaller stability margin and less nose-down authority for stall/spin recovery; (4) page 13 — sweep gives a dihedral effect that grows with CL, i.e. strongest at LOW speed/high AoA, not "at high speeds"; a VENTRAL fin increases directional stability but, being below the roll axis, REDUCES lateral stability; the high-wing "pendulum/keel" picture is a simplification — the main high-wing effect is the sideslip crossflow around the fuselage (CAE Oxford); (5) page 20 — "downward wing creates more lift" is wrong: in a turn the OUTER (upper) wing moves faster and makes more lift, giving the overbanking tendency; (6) page 22 — call it a "stable / neutral spiral MODE" (spirally stable aircraft), not a "stable spiral dive"; (7) page 24 — delete "low yaw rate": a spiral dive has a high turn rate; the key difference from a spin is HIGH and RISING airspeed and g; (8) fleet: C172S and T206H propellers turn clockwise seen from the cockpit → left yaw at high power, right rudder; DA42 HS-NAS engine rotation, critical-engine and yaw-damper status per AFM (SME); CG limits and loading per POH/W&B of each tail (SME); upset/spiral recovery as taught in the D-0507 training manual (SME); (9) remove "[cite: …]" style artefacts if any remain after editing the images.

pages.en: Static stability is the aircraft's initial reaction after it is disturbed from trimmed, straight-and-level flight. If a gust bumps the nose up, the question is: does the aircraft naturally tend to return toward its original attitude, does it stay where it was displaced, or does it keep moving further away? If it tends to return, that is positive static stability. If it simply stays in the new attitude, that is neutral. If the disturbance grows and the aircraft continues away from the original condition, that is negative static stability. Dynamic stability describes what happens over time after that initial reaction. A dynamically stable aircraft shows oscillations that decrease and settle back to equilibrium. If the oscillations keep going at the same size, dynamic stability is neutral. If the oscillations grow, dynamic stability is negative and the motion becomes progressively worse. This motion can be periodic, meaning it oscillates in a repeating pattern, or aperiodic, meaning it returns or diverges without a regular cycle. To talk about stability at all, the aircraft must first be trimmed in equilibrium: lift equals weight, thrust equals drag, and the pitching moments are balanced, so there is no tendency to rotate nose-up or nose-down. When a disturbance occurs, it creates an imbalance. If the aircraft has positive static stability, the aerodynamic forces and moments act as restoring influences that oppose the disturbance. There is also an important trade-off with handling: stability and manoeuvrability are inversely related. More stability generally means the aircraft resists changes more strongly, which reduces manoeuvrability. Less stability makes the aircraft more responsive, but it also demands more attention and precision from the pilot.

pages.on: Infographic: static stability (positive, neutral, negative); manoeuvrability (inversely proportional to stability); dynamic stability (positive, neutral, negative; periodic and aperiodic); combination for equilibrium restoration.
pages.en: Static stability is the aircraft's immediate first reaction after it is disturbed from a trimmed equilibrium condition. If a gust bumps the nose or a wing, static stability answers one question: what is the initial tendency? Does it try to come back, does it stay where it was moved, or does it move further away? With positive static stability the aircraft shows a restoring tendency and begins to return toward the original position. With neutral static stability it simply remains in the new displaced position, without a clear tendency to return or diverge. With negative static stability the disturbance increases and the aircraft initially moves further away from the original condition. Now connect that to manoeuvrability. Manoeuvrability is the aircraft's ability to change its flight path when the pilot applies control inputs. The key relationship is that stability and manoeuvrability are generally inversely proportional. An aircraft designed with higher stability resists change more strongly, so it tends to be less manoeuvrable. An aircraft designed with lower stability is more responsive and manoeuvrable, but it also demands more precise pilot control to keep it where you want it. Next is dynamic stability, which describes what happens over time after the initial reaction. Even if the aircraft initially tends to return, the motion can evolve in different ways. With positive dynamic stability, any oscillations gradually decrease and the aircraft settles back to equilibrium. With neutral dynamic stability, oscillations continue at about the same amplitude. With negative dynamic stability, oscillations grow larger and the motion becomes progressively more divergent. Dynamic motion can be periodic, meaning the aircraft oscillates in a regular, repeating cycle, or aperiodic, meaning it does not repeat — either returning without oscillation or diverging without a repeating pattern. Finally, the combination that best supports safe, predictable handling is positive static stability plus positive dynamic stability. That means the aircraft not only starts to return immediately after a disturbance, but also damps out the motion over time and truly restores the original equilibrium condition.
pages.th: เสถียรภาพสถิตคือปฏิกิริยาแรกทันทีของเครื่องหลังถูกรบกวนจากสภาวะสมดุลที่ trim ไว้ ถ้าลมกระโชกกระทบหัวหรือปีก เสถียรภาพสถิตตอบคำถามเดียว แนวโน้มแรกคืออะไร พยายามกลับ อยู่ที่ตำแหน่งที่ถูกย้ายไป หรือเคลื่อนห่างออกไป เมื่อเสถียรภาพสถิตเป็นบวก เครื่องแสดงแนวโน้มคืนตัวและเริ่มกลับสู่ตำแหน่งเดิม เมื่อเป็นกลาง เครื่องอยู่ที่ตำแหน่งใหม่โดยไม่มีแนวโน้มกลับหรือเบี่ยงออกชัดเจน เมื่อเป็นลบ การรบกวนเพิ่มขึ้นและเครื่องเคลื่อนห่างจากสภาวะเดิมในตอนแรก ทีนี้เชื่อมกับความคล่องตัว ความคล่องตัวคือความสามารถของเครื่องในการเปลี่ยนเส้นทางการบินเมื่อนักบินใช้คันบังคับ ความสัมพันธ์สำคัญคือ เสถียรภาพและความคล่องตัวโดยทั่วไปแปรผกผันกัน เครื่องที่ออกแบบให้เสถียรมากต้านการเปลี่ยนแปลงแรง จึงคล่องตัวน้อยกว่า เครื่องที่ออกแบบให้เสถียรน้อยตอบสนองไวและคล่องตัวกว่า แต่ต้องการการควบคุมที่แม่นยำกว่าเพื่อรักษาไว้ตามต้องการ ต่อไปคือเสถียรภาพพลวัต ซึ่งอธิบายสิ่งที่เกิดตามเวลาหลังปฏิกิริยาแรก แม้เครื่องมีแนวโน้มกลับในตอนแรก การเคลื่อนที่อาจพัฒนาได้หลายแบบ เสถียรภาพพลวัตเป็นบวก การแกว่งค่อย ๆ ลดลงและเครื่องกลับสู่สมดุล เป็นกลาง การแกว่งต่อเนื่องด้วยแอมพลิจูดประมาณเท่าเดิม เป็นลบ การแกว่งใหญ่ขึ้นและเบี่ยงออกมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ การเคลื่อนที่พลวัตอาจเป็น periodic คือแกว่งเป็นรอบซ้ำสม่ำเสมอ หรือ aperiodic คือไม่ซ้ำ กลับโดยไม่แกว่งหรือเบี่ยงออกโดยไม่มีรูปแบบซ้ำ สุดท้าย ส่วนผสมที่ส่งเสริมการบังคับที่ปลอดภัยและคาดเดาได้ที่สุด คือเสถียรภาพสถิตบวกร่วมกับเสถียรภาพพลวัตบวก หมายถึงเครื่องไม่เพียงเริ่มกลับทันทีหลังถูกรบกวน แต่ยังหน่วงการเคลื่อนที่ตามเวลาและกลับสู่สมดุลเดิมได้จริง

pages.on: Text: equilibrium of forces (lift = weight, thrust = drag); equilibrium of moments; static stability concept.
pages.en: Static stability only makes sense if the aircraft starts from a trimmed equilibrium condition. Before any disturbance occurs, the aeroplane must be settled, with no net tendency to accelerate or rotate. First is the equilibrium of forces. In steady, straight-and-level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. That means there is no net vertical force pushing the aircraft up or down, and no net horizontal force making it speed up or slow down. Second is the equilibrium of moments, especially in pitch. The aircraft must have balanced nose-up and nose-down pitching moments, so there is no rotational tendency to pitch the nose higher or lower. This is what trimming does: it sets a condition in which the aircraft can hold a stable attitude and speed without continuous control pressure. Once those force and moment balances exist, the static stability concept becomes clear. A disturbance — turbulence, a gust or a control input — moves the aircraft away from that equilibrium and creates an imbalance. The key question then is: do the resulting aerodynamic forces and moments act as restoring effects or not? With positive static stability, the disturbance produces restoring forces and moments that oppose the displacement. For example, if the nose is disturbed upward, the aircraft's aerodynamic response tends to generate a nose-down restoring moment that drives it back toward the original trimmed condition. If the response neither restores nor diverges, stability is neutral. If the response reinforces the displacement, stability is negative. So the precondition is simple: start at equilibrium, then evaluate whether the aircraft's immediate reaction to a disturbance produces restoring forces and moments that return it toward that equilibrium.

pages.en: Pitch balance is achieved by making sure the aircraft's total pitching moments add up to zero, so the nose has no tendency to rotate up or down. The main tools that create that balance are the tail or a canard, the relative positions of the CG and the wing's centre of pressure, and then the pilot's controls and power setting. A stabiliser on a conventional tailplane typically provides the balancing force by producing a downward aerodynamic force. That downward force, acting well behind the centre of gravity, creates the nose-up moment needed to counter the wing and fuselage pitching tendencies and keep the aircraft trimmed. In a canard configuration the balancing surface is in front of the CG and generally produces an upward force, providing the required pitching moment from the front instead of the rear. The position of the wing's centre of pressure (CP) relative to the centre of gravity (CG) affects how much balancing force is required. When the CP is aft of the CG, the lift-weight couple gives a nose-down tendency that requires the stabiliser to provide a greater downward force to maintain equilibrium. If the CP shifts forward of the CG, the balance requirement changes, and depending on configuration and design the stabiliser may need to produce less downward force, or in some cases an upward force, to maintain the correct pitching-moment balance. Airspeed matters because aerodynamic force increases with dynamic pressure. As speed increases, the stabiliser or canard becomes more effective and the same deflection generates a larger balancing force, which is why trim and pitch feel change with speed. The pilot fine-tunes this balance with elevator deflection. Moving the elevator changes the stabiliser's effective camber and angle of attack, increasing or decreasing the force it produces, which directly adjusts the pitching moment and controls the pitch attitude. Finally, thrust changes can create pitching moments through thrust-line offset, slipstream effects over the tail, or changes in drag. When power is increased or reduced the aircraft may pitch up or down, and the pilot uses elevator, and often retrims, to compensate and restore the balanced, trimmed condition.

pages.en: Static longitudinal stability is about how the aircraft responds in pitch when the angle of attack is disturbed away from its trimmed value. The key question is: after a disturbance, does the aircraft generate a pitching moment that opposes the change and pushes it back toward equilibrium? If the angle of attack increases, lift increases immediately, but what matters for stability is the resulting pitching moment. In a positively statically stable aircraft, an increase in angle of attack produces a nose-down restoring moment. That nose-down tendency reduces the angle of attack again and drives the aircraft back toward the trimmed condition. If the angle of attack decreases, lift decreases and a stable aircraft generates the opposite response, a nose-up restoring moment. That nose-up tendency increases the angle of attack back toward the trim value. So for positive static longitudinal stability, the aircraft must produce a pitching moment that always opposes the angle-of-attack disturbance: AoA up gives nose down; AoA down gives nose up. The centre-of-gravity position has a major influence on how strongly this restoring tendency acts, and it also affects handling. With a forward CG the aircraft generally becomes more stable, because the CG is further ahead of the neutral point and the tail has a longer arm to generate a restoring moment. The trade-off is reduced manoeuvrability and typically heavier pitch control forces, because the aircraft resists changes more. With an aft CG the aircraft becomes less stable, because the restoring moment arm is reduced. That usually makes the aircraft feel more responsive and more manoeuvrable, but it also reduces the margin of stability: small disturbances or control inputs can produce larger pitch changes, and recovery from upsets can be more demanding. So the core message is: static longitudinal stability is about the restoring pitch moment after an angle-of-attack change, and the CG position shifts the balance between stability and manoeuvrability.

pages.en: The neutral point is the centre-of-gravity location at which the aircraft has neutral static longitudinal stability. At this point, if the angle of attack is disturbed from trim, the aircraft produces no restoring pitching moment: it neither tends to return toward the original condition nor to diverge further. In practical terms the aircraft would feel very sensitive in pitch and would not self-correct after small disturbances. The neutral point is not an arbitrary value. It is determined mainly by the aircraft's aerodynamic design, especially the relationship between the wing and the tail. Key contributors include the wing's aerodynamic characteristics, the tail's size and effectiveness, the tail moment arm — the distance from the CG to the tail — and how downwash from the wing affects the tail. Because these are design features, the neutral point is essentially fixed for a given configuration, while the aircraft's actual CG can move forward or aft depending on loading. This leads to an important operational idea: the distance between the actual CG and the neutral point is the static margin. With the CG forward of the neutral point, the aircraft has positive static stability. As the CG moves aft toward the neutral point, stability decreases. If the CG moves aft of the neutral point, the aircraft becomes statically unstable.

pages.t: Factors Affecting Neutral Point (NP) in Aircraft
pages.on: Infographic: 1 relative locations (wing and tail/canard ACs); 2 downwash influence (NP shifts forward at high AoA); 3 engine nacelles contribution.
pages.en: The neutral point is set mainly by how the wing and the tail or canard share the job of producing lift and pitching moments, so several design and flow effects can shift where it effectively sits. Relative locations: the neutral point typically lies somewhere between the aerodynamic centre of the wing and the aerodynamic centre of the tail or canard. If the tail becomes more effective — because it is larger, further from the CG, or operating in cleaner airflow — the neutral point moves aft, which allows the aircraft to remain stable with a more aft CG. If the tail is less effective, the neutral point moves forward, reducing the stability margin. Downwash influence: as angle of attack increases, the wing produces stronger circulation and the downwash behind the wing increases. That downwash reduces the effective angle of attack seen by the tail, which can reduce tail effectiveness. When the tail becomes less effective, the aircraft's overall restoring tendency in pitch is reduced and the neutral point shifts forward, meaning you need a more forward CG to keep the same static stability margin. Engine nacelles' contribution: engine nacelles are not aerodynamically neutral. They can generate lift and, more importantly, pitching moments, especially at higher angles of attack and in disturbed flow. Depending on nacelle shape, position relative to the wing, and how their flow interacts with the wing and tail, the nacelles can add a nose-up or nose-down tendency that changes the aircraft's overall pitching-moment curve. That changes the balance of moments that defines stability, and therefore can shift the neutral point forward or aft — nacelles ahead of the wing are generally destabilising. Bottom line: the neutral point is a design-driven location, but it can move with configuration and airflow effects, especially those that change tail effectiveness or add extra pitching moments.

pages.t: Aircraft Centre of Gravity (CG): Influence and Limits
pages.on: Infographic: forward CG (positive static stability, reduced manoeuvrability); aft CG ("negative static stability"); CG limits and effects (control forces, elevator effectiveness, stability); static margin.
pages.en: The centre-of-gravity location is one of the biggest drivers of longitudinal stability and handling, because it changes how much balancing moment the tail or canard must produce and how much margin the aircraft has before it becomes neutrally stable. With a forward CG the aircraft has stronger positive static stability. After a pitch disturbance it produces a clearer restoring moment, so it naturally returns toward the trimmed condition. The trade-off is reduced manoeuvrability and higher pilot effort. Because the tail must generate a larger balancing moment, the elevator typically needs more deflection to achieve the same pitch change, and the pilot will notice heavier control forces, especially in slow flight and during the flare. This is why a forward CG can increase pilot workload even though it improves stability. With an aft CG, stability decreases as the CG moves closer to the neutral point. The aircraft becomes more responsive, so it may feel more manoeuvrable, but it also becomes easier to over-control and less willing to self-correct after disturbances. If the CG goes too far aft, the aircraft can reach neutral or even negative static stability, meaning it may not naturally return to the trimmed condition. An aft CG also affects control margins: although the aircraft may feel lighter on the controls, the elevator may not have enough nose-down authority when it matters most. In operational terms an aft CG can reduce control authority for recovery from high-angle-of-attack situations, such as stalls and spins. CG limits exist to keep the aircraft within safe ranges of control force, elevator effectiveness and stability. Forward CG: higher control forces, more stable, but it can demand more elevator to flare or rotate. Aft CG: lower control forces, less stable, and it can reduce the margin for recovery and make the aircraft more sensitive. A useful way to quantify this is the static margin — the distance between the CG and the neutral point, expressed as a percentage of the mean aerodynamic chord (MAC). A larger static margin, with the CG further forward of the neutral point, means more static stability; a smaller static margin means less stability and more sensitivity.

pages.on: Infographic: phugoid (long period, lightly damped, speed/altitude exchange, AoA ≈ constant) and short period (heavily damped, pitch/AoA); risks: PIO, altitude effects, CG location influence.
pages.en: Dynamic longitudinal stability describes how the aircraft's pitch-related motion develops over time after a disturbance. In practice we talk about two natural modes: the phugoid and the short period. The phugoid is a long-period, lightly damped oscillation. It shows up as a slow exchange between airspeed and altitude: the aircraft speeds up as it descends, then slows down as it climbs. During a classic phugoid the angle of attack stays nearly constant, so the motion is more about energy exchange than rapid pitch changes. Because it is lightly damped, it can persist for a while unless the pilot intervenes or the damping is strong. The short-period mode is the opposite: short period and heavily damped. It involves quick changes in pitch attitude and angle of attack with minimal change in speed. This mode is especially important because it is the one you feel immediately after a control input — how crisp or stable the aircraft feels in pitch. A well-damped short-period response makes the aircraft easier to fly precisely, especially in turbulence and on the approach. A problem related to the short-period response is pilot-induced oscillation, PIO. PIO happens when the pilot unintentionally gets into a rhythm of over-correcting, often because the aircraft's response lags slightly behind the pilot's input. Each correction arrives a bit late and can amplify the oscillation instead of stopping it. Smooth, appropriately timed inputs and an understanding of the aircraft's pitch response are the key prevention. Altitude also matters. At higher altitudes air density is lower, which reduces aerodynamic damping. With less natural damping, oscillations decay more slowly and the aircraft can feel more 'floaty' in pitch, increasing susceptibility to unwanted oscillations. Finally, the CG location strongly influences damping and stability. A forward CG generally increases the restoring tendency and improves damping, making the aircraft more stable in pitch. An aft CG reduces stability and damping, making the pitch response more sensitive and increasing the risk that oscillations — especially short-period and PIO — build rather than settle.
pages.th: เสถียรภาพพลวัตตามยาวอธิบายการเคลื่อนที่ทางก้มเงยของเครื่องตามเวลาหลังถูกรบกวน ในทางปฏิบัติพูดถึงสองโหมดธรรมชาติ คือ phugoid และ short period phugoid เป็นการแกว่งคาบยาวที่หน่วงน้อย ปรากฏเป็นการแลกเปลี่ยนช้า ๆ ระหว่างความเร็วกับความสูง เครื่องเร็วขึ้นเมื่อลดระดับ แล้วช้าลงเมื่อไต่ ใน phugoid แบบคลาสสิก มุมปะทะเกือบคงที่ การเคลื่อนที่จึงเป็นเรื่องการแลกเปลี่ยนพลังงานมากกว่าการเปลี่ยนท่าทางรวดเร็ว เพราะหน่วงน้อยจึงอาจคงอยู่นานถ้านักบินไม่แทรกแซงหรือการหน่วงไม่แรง โหมด short period ตรงข้าม คาบสั้นและหน่วงมาก เป็นการเปลี่ยนท่าทางก้มเงยและมุมปะทะอย่างรวดเร็ว โดยความเร็วเปลี่ยนน้อยมาก โหมดนี้สำคัญเป็นพิเศษเพราะเป็นสิ่งที่รู้สึกทันทีหลังใช้คันบังคับ คือเครื่องรู้สึกคมหรือนิ่งแค่ไหนทางก้มเงย short period ที่หน่วงดีทำให้บินได้แม่นยำง่ายขึ้น โดยเฉพาะในอากาศแปรปรวนและตอน approach ปัญหาที่เกี่ยวกับการตอบสนอง short period คือ pilot-induced oscillation (PIO) เกิดเมื่อนักบินเข้าจังหวะแก้เกินโดยไม่ตั้งใจ มักเพราะการตอบสนองของเครื่องช้ากว่าการบังคับเล็กน้อย การแก้แต่ละครั้งมาช้าไปนิดและอาจขยายการแกว่งแทนที่จะหยุด การบังคับที่นุ่มนวลและจังหวะเหมาะสม รวมถึงการเข้าใจการตอบสนองทางก้มเงยของเครื่อง คือการป้องกันหลัก ความสูงก็มีผล ที่สูงความหนาแน่นอากาศต่ำลง การหน่วงทางอากาศพลศาสตร์ลดลง การแกว่งจึงลดลงช้ากว่า และเครื่องอาจรู้สึก 'ลอย ๆ' ทางก้มเงย เสี่ยงต่อการแกว่งที่ไม่ต้องการมากขึ้น สุดท้าย ตำแหน่ง CG มีอิทธิพลมากต่อการหน่วงและเสถียรภาพ CG ค่อนหน้ามักเพิ่มแนวโน้มคืนตัวและการหน่วง เครื่องเสถียรทางก้มเงยมากขึ้น CG ค่อนหลังลดเสถียรภาพและการหน่วง การตอบสนองทางก้มเงยไวขึ้น และเพิ่มความเสี่ยงที่การแกว่ง โดยเฉพาะ short period และ PIO จะสะสมแทนที่จะสงบลง

pages.on: Infographic: definition (restoring yaw moment); weak stability (sensitive, workload); strong stability (sluggish, difficult to manoeuvre).
pages.en: Static directional stability is the aircraft's immediate yaw response after a disturbance. If a gust yaws the nose left or right, static directional stability describes whether the aircraft naturally produces a restoring yawing moment that tends to point the nose back into the relative wind and return toward the original yaw condition — the 'weathercock' effect, produced mainly by the fin and the fuselage side area behind the CG. When directional stability is weak, the aircraft is more sensitive to yaw disturbances. Small gusts or minor control inputs can cause noticeable yaw excursions, and the aircraft may require frequent rudder corrections to stay aligned, especially in turbulence, in the climb or at low speeds. That sensitivity increases pilot workload, and it can also make coordination in turns more demanding. When directional stability is strong, the restoring tendency is pronounced, so the aircraft strongly wants to align with the airflow. This can reduce the need for constant small corrections, but the trade-off is that the yaw response can feel sluggish. The aircraft may resist yaw changes, requiring more rudder input to initiate or change a manoeuvre, and it can feel less agile, particularly in tasks where quick heading changes or precise yaw control are needed. So the balance is important: enough directional stability to damp yaw disturbances naturally and keep the aircraft tracking straight, but not so much that the aircraft becomes difficult to manoeuvre smoothly.
pages.th: เสถียรภาพสถิตทางทิศทางคือการตอบสนองทาง yaw ทันทีของเครื่องหลังถูกรบกวน ถ้าลมกระโชกทำให้หัวหันซ้ายหรือขวา เสถียรภาพนี้อธิบายว่าเครื่องสร้างโมเมนต์หันคืนตัวเองหรือไม่ ที่ชี้หัวกลับเข้าหาลมสัมพัทธ์และกลับสู่ทิศเดิม คือผล 'ไก่ลม' (weathercock) ซึ่งเกิดจากครีบหางและพื้นที่ด้านข้างของลำตัวหลัง CG เป็นหลัก เมื่อเสถียรภาพทางทิศทางอ่อน เครื่องไวต่อการรบกวนทาง yaw ลมกระโชกเล็กน้อยหรือการบังคับเพียงนิดก็ทำให้หัวส่ายชัดเจน และอาจต้องแก้ด้วย rudder บ่อยเพื่อให้ตรงแนว โดยเฉพาะในอากาศแปรปรวน ขณะไต่ หรือที่ความเร็วต่ำ ความไวนี้เพิ่มภาระงานนักบิน และทำให้การประสานคันบังคับในการเลี้ยวยากขึ้น เมื่อเสถียรภาพทางทิศทางแรง แนวโน้มคืนตัวชัดเจน เครื่องอยากตรงกับกระแสอากาศมาก ลดความจำเป็นในการแก้เล็ก ๆ ต่อเนื่อง แต่สิ่งที่แลกคือการตอบสนองทาง yaw อาจรู้สึกเฉื่อย เครื่องอาจต้านการเปลี่ยน yaw ต้องใช้ rudder มากขึ้นเพื่อเริ่มหรือเปลี่ยน manoeuvre และรู้สึกคล่องตัวน้อยลง โดยเฉพาะงานที่ต้องเปลี่ยนทิศเร็วหรือควบคุม yaw แม่นยำ สมดุลจึงสำคัญ มีเสถียรภาพทางทิศทางพอจะหน่วงการรบกวน yaw ตามธรรมชาติและให้เครื่องบินตรง แต่ไม่มากจนบังคับอย่างนุ่มนวลได้ยาก

pages.on: Infographic: definition (restoring roll moment toward original bank); weak stability (sensitive to turbulence, constant corrections); strong stability (resistant to bank changes, reduced manoeuvrability).
pages.en: Static lateral stability is the aircraft's immediate rolling response after a disturbance in bank. If turbulence tips a wing down, static lateral stability describes whether the aircraft naturally generates a restoring rolling moment that tends to bring the wings back toward the original bank angle — typically back toward wings level. Note that the restoring moment does not come from the bank itself but from the sideslip that the bank produces. When lateral stability is weak, the aircraft is more sensitive to turbulence: small disturbances can produce noticeable and persistent bank changes, so the pilot often has to make frequent aileron corrections to keep the wings where desired. That increases workload and can make precise tracking, like holding a heading in bumpy air, more demanding. When lateral stability is strong, the aircraft tends to resist changes in bank. After a disturbance it more strongly tries to roll back toward its trimmed condition, which can make the aircraft feel steady and less twitchy. The trade-off is reduced manoeuvrability: stronger lateral stability means the aircraft may need more control input to establish or change a bank angle, and it can feel less responsive during roll-in and roll-out. So, as for the other axes, lateral stability is a balance: enough restoring tendency to reduce unwanted rolling from turbulence, but not so much that it becomes difficult to manoeuvre smoothly and precisely.
pages.th: เสถียรภาพสถิตทางข้างคือการตอบสนองทางการเอียงทันทีของเครื่องหลังถูกรบกวนมุมเอียง ถ้าอากาศแปรปรวนทำให้ปีกข้างหนึ่งตก เสถียรภาพนี้อธิบายว่าเครื่องสร้างโมเมนต์เอียงคืนตัวเองหรือไม่ ที่พาปีกกลับสู่มุมเอียงเดิม ปกติคือกลับสู่ปีกระดับ สังเกตว่าโมเมนต์คืนตัวไม่ได้มาจากการเอียงโดยตรง แต่มาจาก sideslip ที่การเอียงทำให้เกิด เมื่อเสถียรภาพทางข้างอ่อน เครื่องไวต่ออากาศแปรปรวน การรบกวนเล็กน้อยทำให้มุมเอียงเปลี่ยนชัดเจนและค้างอยู่ นักบินจึงต้องแก้ด้วย aileron บ่อยเพื่อรักษาปีกตามต้องการ เพิ่มภาระงาน และทำให้การบินแม่นยำ เช่นรักษาทิศในอากาศแปรปรวนยากขึ้น เมื่อเสถียรภาพทางข้างแรง เครื่องต้านการเปลี่ยนมุมเอียง หลังถูกรบกวนจะพยายามเอียงกลับสู่สภาวะที่ trim ไว้แรงขึ้น ทำให้เครื่องรู้สึกนิ่งและไม่กระตุก สิ่งที่แลกคือความคล่องตัวลดลง เสถียรภาพทางข้างที่แรงหมายถึงอาจต้องใช้คันบังคับมากขึ้นเพื่อเข้าหรือเปลี่ยนมุมเอียง และรู้สึกตอบสนองน้อยลงตอนเข้าและออกจากการเอียง ดังนั้นเช่นเดียวกับแกนอื่น เสถียรภาพทางข้างคือความสมดุล มีแนวโน้มคืนตัวพอจะลดการเอียงที่ไม่ต้องการจากอากาศแปรปรวน แต่ไม่มากจนบังคับอย่างนุ่มนวลและแม่นยำได้ยาก
pages.kEn: Lateral stability is driven by sideslip: bank → sideslip toward the low wing → restoring roll (dihedral effect).
pages.kTh: เสถียรภาพทางข้างขับเคลื่อนด้วย sideslip: เอียง → sideslip ไปทางปีกต่ำ → โมเมนต์เอียงคืนตัว (dihedral effect)
pages.gEn: Show it in the C172S: in smooth air, bank 10° and release the ailerons with feet off — the high wing and dihedral slowly reduce the bank (or the spiral mode takes over — page 22). Check: why does a perfectly coordinated (no sideslip) bank produce no lateral restoring moment?

pages.on: Infographic: 1 dihedral/anhedral; 2 wing position (high-wing "keel effect", low wing); 3 sweep angle ("especially at high speeds"); 4 ventral fin ("adds lateral stability"); 5 vertical tail; dihedral effect key mechanism.
pages.en: Static lateral stability comes from design features that create a restoring rolling moment when the aircraft is disturbed into a bank and starts to sideslip. Several geometric elements contribute. Dihedral and anhedral are the most direct. With dihedral — wings angled upward from the fuselage — the aircraft develops a stronger dihedral effect: in a sideslip the lower, into-wind wing meets the airflow at a slightly higher angle of attack, producing more lift than the higher wing. That lift difference creates a rolling moment back toward wings level, increasing lateral stability. Anhedral — wings angled downward — reduces this effect, and is often used when designers want less lateral stability and more roll responsiveness. Wing position also matters. A high-wing aircraft tends to be more laterally stable. The simple 'pendulum' or 'keel' picture says the fuselage hanging below the wing swings it back; the main aerodynamic reason is that in a sideslip the crossflow around the fuselage raises the angle of attack at the root of the into-wind high wing and lowers it on the other side, giving a restoring roll. Low-wing aircraft get the opposite effect, so designers give them more dihedral to achieve the desired stability. Sweep angle adds lateral stability: in a sideslip the into-wind wing effectively has less sweep and generates more lift than the other wing, creating a stabilising rolling tendency. This effect grows with lift coefficient, so it is strongest at low speed and high angle of attack — swept wings can have too much dihedral effect at low speed. A ventral fin — a fin below the fuselage near the tail — adds side area low on the aircraft. In a sideslip it produces a side force that adds directional stability, but because it acts below the roll axis it slightly reduces lateral stability. Finally, the vertical tail is crucial. While it is primarily associated with directional stability, it also influences lateral behaviour because yaw and roll are coupled. When the aircraft yaws or slips, the vertical tail, which sits above the roll axis, generates a side force that also produces a rolling moment, and it controls the sideslip that drives the dihedral effect. In summary, static lateral stability is largely about how the aircraft responds to sideslip and bank: features like dihedral, a high wing and sweep increase the restoring tendency, while anhedral, a low wing and a ventral fin reduce it.

pages.on: Infographic: 1 coupled motions (roll ↔ yaw); 2 damping (decaying oscillation; tail surfaces provide damping); 3 Dutch roll (yaw and roll oscillation, common in swept-wing aircraft).
pages.en: Dynamic lateral and directional stability are closely linked, because roll and yaw are coupled in real flight. A disturbance in one axis often triggers motion in the other. For example, a yaw disturbance creates a sideslip, and sideslip can generate a rolling moment through the dihedral effect. Likewise, a roll disturbance can change the lift distribution and induce yaw through adverse yaw. Because of this coupling, pilots often feel lateral-directional behaviour as one combined response rather than two separate ones. Whether the aircraft settles down or continues to oscillate depends largely on damping. Damping is the set of aerodynamic forces and moments that oppose motion, like aerodynamic friction. In yaw, damping comes mainly from the vertical tail, which resists yaw rate and helps align the aircraft with the relative wind. In roll, damping comes mainly from the wings: the down-going wing meets the air at a higher angle of attack and the up-going wing at a lower one, which opposes the roll rate. When damping is strong, the aircraft returns to equilibrium quickly after a disturbance. When damping is weak, oscillations decay slowly, or in the worst case can grow. A classic coupled lateral-directional motion is Dutch roll. Dutch roll is an oscillation that combines yawing and rolling: the nose swings left and right while the wings rock, typically out of phase. It often starts with a yaw disturbance, like turbulence, that produces a sideslip. The dihedral effect then converts that sideslip into a roll response. As the aircraft rolls, the yaw dynamics and tail forces interact and the cycle can repeat. In many training aircraft it is naturally well damped, but in some aircraft — especially those with strong lateral stability (dihedral effect) relative to their directional stability, such as swept-wing jets — Dutch roll can persist and may require pilot input or a yaw damper to control. So the key ideas are: roll and yaw are interconnected, damping determines whether the motion decays, and Dutch roll is the recognisable yaw-roll oscillation that results from that coupling.

pages.t: Aircraft Coupled Motions: Stability and Axes of Rotation
pages.on: Infographic: coupled motions (lateral ↔ directional); yaw (vertical axis), roll (longitudinal axis), pitch (lateral axis).
pages.en: Coupled motions mean the aircraft's axes do not behave in isolation. Lateral and directional stability in particular are tightly linked, so a disturbance that starts as yaw often turns into roll, and a roll input can create yaw. That coupling is why pilots fly turns with coordinated aileron and rudder, not with aileron alone. Yaw is rotation about the vertical (normal) axis: the nose swings left or right. A yaw disturbance usually creates a sideslip, meaning the airflow is no longer aligned straight with the nose. That sideslip is important, because it becomes the trigger for other motions. Roll is rotation about the longitudinal axis: one wing goes down and the other goes up. When the aircraft is sideslipping, design features like dihedral, sweep and wing position create a rolling moment, often rolling the aircraft in a direction that tries to reduce the slip. Roll can also produce yaw through adverse yaw, where the down-going aileron increases lift and drag on that wing and pulls the nose the opposite way — another example of coupling. Pitch is rotation about the lateral axis: the nose moves up or down. Pitch is not the main axis in lateral-directional coupling, but it still interacts indirectly, because changes in pitch affect airspeed and angle of attack, which change how strongly the aerodynamic forces in yaw and roll act. So the takeaway is: yaw disturbances create sideslip, sideslip drives roll, and roll inputs can drive yaw. These interactions are what we mean by coupled motions.

pages.on: Infographic: 1 aerodynamic damping (air resistance, wing shape); 2 structural damping (internal friction in fuselage, control surfaces); key takeaway.
pages.en: Damping is the set of effects that oppose motion and help the aircraft settle back to equilibrium after a disturbance. Without damping, an aircraft displaced from its trimmed condition could keep oscillating for a long time, or in some cases the oscillations could grow. With good damping, the motion naturally decays and the aircraft returns to steady flight with less pilot input. Aerodynamic damping is the dominant type in flight. It comes from the way the airflow resists changes in motion, especially rates of motion. When the aircraft starts to yaw, roll or pitch, different parts of the airframe experience changed local angles of attack, creating forces that tend to oppose that rate. For example, in yaw the vertical tail is especially important: as the aircraft yaws, the tail develops a resisting side force that counters the yaw rate and helps align the nose with the relative wind. In roll, the wings generate forces that oppose the roll rate. In pitch, the tailplane does the same as the nose moves up or down. The stronger these rate-opposing forces, the faster oscillations decay. Structural damping comes from the aircraft itself — how the structure absorbs and dissipates energy through small flexing and internal friction in components such as the fuselage, control linkages and surfaces. Compared with aerodynamic damping, structural damping is usually small in normal flight dynamics, but it still contributes to reducing vibration, and it can help prevent certain oscillations from persisting or becoming uncomfortable. So the big picture is: aerodynamic damping is the primary stabilising brake on motion in the air, while structural damping provides additional energy absorption within the aircraft, both working together to reduce oscillations and restore stable flight.

pages.en: Asymmetric propeller slipstream happens because the propwash leaving the propeller is not straight: it spirals around the fuselage and strikes the tail surfaces unevenly. In high-power, low-speed situations like take-off, climb and go-around, that uneven flow becomes much more noticeable, because the propwash is stronger and spirals more tightly, and the aircraft is often at a higher angle of attack. The first effect is yaw. One side of the vertical tail receives the spiralling slipstream more strongly than the other, creating an unbalanced side force. The yawing tendency is strongest at high power and low airspeed. In single-engine training aircraft with a propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, the slipstream strikes the left side of the fin, so the aircraft tends to yaw left at high power, and the pilot needs right rudder to keep the nose aligned. The second effect is roll. If one wing experiences more energised airflow than the other, it can produce slightly different lift and drag, and the aircraft may roll toward one side; together with engine torque this can show up as a need for light aileron pressure to keep the wings level during the initial climb. The third effect is pitch. Depending on how the spiral slipstream strikes the horizontal tail, and how thrust changes the airflow over the tail, the aircraft can show a pitch tendency, pitching up or down with power changes. The key point is that the pitch response can change with configuration, speed and power. The pilot response is proactive: anticipate the yaw, use rudder first to stay coordinated and maintain the runway track, and use aileron as needed to hold the wings level. During take-off, increase right rudder as power comes in. During the climb, maintain continuous coordinated pressure. During a go-around, apply immediate rudder and attitude control at the same time as power, to prevent a sudden yaw and roll.

pages.t: Coupling of Lateral and Directional Stability
pages.on: Infographic: 1 lateral influencing directional (dihedral effect, adverse yaw); 2 directional influencing lateral (vertical tail side force → rolling tendency); 3 integrated dynamic response (stability augmentation).
pages.en: Lateral and directional stability work as a combined system, because roll, yaw and sideslip are constantly interacting. In real flight a disturbance in one axis rarely stays pure: it quickly creates effects in the other axis through sideslip and aerodynamic coupling. Roll influencing yaw: when the aircraft banks, the lift vector tilts and the aircraft begins to turn. But roll can also create yaw through secondary aerodynamic effects. Aileron inputs produce adverse yaw, because the down-going aileron increases lift and drag on that wing, pulling the nose opposite to the intended turn. In addition, when a banked aircraft develops sideslip, the dihedral effect and wing geometry can produce unequal lift and drag between the wings, which contributes to yaw tendencies that must be managed with rudder. The practical result is that roll changes require rudder coordination to keep the nose aligned with the flight path. Yaw influencing roll: a yaw disturbance typically produces sideslip — the relative wind strikes the aircraft from the side. In a sideslip, the wing and tail geometry generate a rolling moment: dihedral, sweep and wing position often cause the aircraft to roll in response to sideslip as it tries to return toward aligned flight. The vertical tail also plays a major role. When it is exposed to a sideslip it generates a side force to correct the yaw, and because the fin sits above the roll axis, that side force also creates a rolling tendency. Integrated dynamic response: because roll and yaw continuously influence each other, the aircraft can develop coupled oscillations such as Dutch roll, where yaw and roll alternate in a repeating pattern. Whether this motion quickly settles or persists depends largely on damping and on the balance between directional stability and tail effectiveness on one side, and lateral stability, dihedral effect and roll damping on the other. In many aircraft the oscillation is naturally well damped; in others it may require pilot technique or stability augmentation, such as a yaw damper, to reduce workload and maintain smooth, precise flight. The operational takeaway is simple: treat roll and yaw as a team. The bank controls the turn, but the rudder keeps the aircraft aligned and prevents the coupling from turning into unwanted oscillations.

pages.t: Dutch Roll: A Coupled Oscillation of Yaw and Roll
pages.on: Infographic: yaw (nose swings left and right) and roll (banks left and right) around a figure-of-eight path.
pages.en: Dutch roll is a coupled lateral-directional oscillation, meaning yaw and roll feed into each other instead of happening separately. The aircraft alternates between a side-to-side nose motion and a left-right banking motion, creating a repeating cycle. It typically starts with a yaw disturbance — for example, turbulence yaws the nose off the flight path. That yaw creates a sideslip, so the relative wind is no longer coming straight into the nose. Once the aircraft is slipping, the lateral stability features — especially the dihedral effect and sometimes wing sweep — produce a rolling response. The aircraft then banks, and that bank creates additional yaw effects through aerodynamic coupling and tail forces. As the aircraft tries to correct itself it overshoots, setting up the next part of the cycle. So the two visible components are: yaw — the nose swings left and right as the aeroplane alternately points slightly into the airflow and then past it; and roll — the aircraft banks left and right, out of phase with the yaw, as the wings respond to the sideslip and the aircraft's attempt to restabilise. The key safety point is that Dutch roll is mainly about comfort and workload in most training aircraft, because it is usually well damped. But if damping is weak, the oscillation can persist and may require pilot technique — smooth inputs and coordination — or, in some aircraft, a yaw damper to suppress the yaw component and break the cycle.

pages.t: Spiral Dive: A Dangerous, Descending, Tightening Flight Condition
pages.on: Infographic: 1 yaw (nose swings, "asymmetric lift", adverse yaw); 2 roll (bank steepens, "downward wing creates more lift"); 3 pitch (nose down, speed up); recovery: reduce power, level wings, gently pull out.
pages.en: A spiral dive is an unintentional, tightening, descending turn in which bank angle and airspeed both increase. It most often develops when the pilot loses accurate attitude reference — in haze, cloud or at night — and the aircraft slowly enters a bank that goes unnoticed. Because the aircraft is not stalled, it can accelerate rapidly, and that makes this condition structurally dangerous. The motion is driven by a coupled set of effects. Yaw: as the aircraft begins to turn, yaw and sideslip can build. If the turn is not fully coordinated, the nose swings and the airflow no longer meets the aircraft straight on; that sideslip can aggravate the turn and make control feel messy, especially as speed builds. Roll: the aircraft remains banked, and the outer wing, travelling faster on the larger radius, produces more lift than the inner wing — the overbanking tendency — so if the pilot does not correct the bank, the turn continues to tighten into a spiral. The aircraft is in a steepening turn where the lift vector is tilted and its vertical component is not enough to hold altitude. The aircraft descends, the turn tightens, and the increasing airspeed raises the load factor, so the aircraft can feel as if it is pulling into the turn. Pitch: as the aircraft descends, the nose is typically down and the aircraft accelerates. Unlike a stall-spin scenario, where airspeed is low, a spiral dive is characterised by high and increasing airspeed and a rapidly increasing descent rate. If uncorrected, airspeed and g-loading can exceed the aircraft's limits. Recovery must be done in the right order to avoid overstressing the airframe. One: reduce power to stop further acceleration. Two: level the wings using coordinated aileron and rudder — this is the priority, because pulling while still banked increases load factor dramatically and only tightens the spiral. Three: once the wings are level, gently raise the nose to recover to level flight, avoiding an abrupt pull-up that could produce excessive g at high speed. The key training lesson is recognition: a spiral dive is a high-speed, tightening, descending turn, and the safest fix is power back, wings level, then recover the pitch smoothly.

pages.t: Understanding Spiral Divergence: A Lateral-Directional Instability
pages.on: Infographic: 1 the set-up (strong directional, weak lateral stability); 2 the progression (coupled motion); 3 the spiral (tightening, descending turn); practical recognition and prevention.
pages.en: Spiral divergence is a lateral-directional instability in which a small disturbance can slowly develop into a tightening, descending turn if it is not corrected. The classic set-up is strong static directional stability combined with weak static lateral stability. With high directional stability, the vertical tail strongly weathercocks the aircraft toward the relative wind. That sounds good, but it also means any small sideslip produces a strong corrective yawing moment that turns the nose into the slip — into the turn. Because yaw and roll are coupled, that yaw makes the outer wing move faster and produces a rolling moment that increases the bank. If lateral stability is low, the aircraft does not generate a strong enough restoring roll moment back toward wings level, so when the yaw produces a slight roll, the aircraft does not naturally stop it. The bank angle can then persist and gradually increase. Once bank is present, the aircraft begins to turn. Turning introduces more sideslip and yaw tendencies and changes the aerodynamic balance again, so the aircraft 'chases' its own corrections: yaw generates roll, roll leads to a turn, the turn produces more sideslip, and the cycle continues. As the bank increases, the vertical component of lift decreases, so the aircraft starts to descend, and airspeed builds if power is not reduced — turning the situation into a potentially hazardous spiral dive if the pilot remains unaware or delays the correction. The practical recognition cue is a slowly increasing bank and a developing turn that does not feel dramatic at first, often noticed as a heading drift, an increasing descent rate or rising airspeed. The practical prevention is disciplined attitude control: stop the bank early, stay coordinated, and maintain a reliable attitude reference, especially when outside visual cues are weak.

pages.t: Conditions for Neutral or Stable Spiral Dive Mode
pages.on: Infographic: neutral spiral (lateral and directional balanced → constant bank and airspeed); stable spiral (high lateral stability → bank and airspeed gradually decrease); key takeaway.
pages.en: The spiral mode describes what happens over time after the aircraft is disturbed into a small bank and allowed to find its own behaviour with the controls free. Whether the bank tightens, stays about the same, or slowly unwinds depends mainly on the balance between lateral stability and directional stability, and on how strongly yaw-roll coupling feeds the motion. A neutral spiral mode occurs when the lateral and directional effects are balanced. A small bank creates a gentle turn, but the aircraft's natural tendencies do not strongly amplify or cancel it. The aircraft can remain in a steady, shallow, descending turn with bank angle and airspeed approximately constant. It will not quickly self-correct back to wings level, but it will not rapidly tighten on its own either. From a pilot's perspective this still requires monitoring, because if anything changes — turbulence, speed, power — the balance can shift and a spiral can begin to develop. A stable spiral mode occurs when the aircraft has stronger lateral stability, meaning a clear restoring tendency to roll back toward wings level. Here lateral stability is strong enough to overcome the yaw-roll coupling that would otherwise sustain the turn. After the disturbance the aircraft gradually reduces bank, the turn rate decreases, and the aircraft trends back toward straight flight. As the bank decreases, the descent and airspeed tendency also reduce, so the aircraft naturally returns toward level flight, assuming power and trim remain unchanged and the aircraft is not being held in the turn. The key takeaway is that spiral behaviour is not just 'bank equals turn': it is about whether the aircraft's design produces a net tendency to amplify, maintain or damp out the bank over time. Neutral means the bank tends to persist; stable means it tends to self-correct back toward wings level.

pages.t: Unstable Spiral Dive Mode: Characteristics and Dangers
pages.on: Infographic: 1 bank angle (continues to increase); 2 airspeed (increases); 3 pitch attitude (nose-low); 4 altitude (rapid loss); real-world example and recovery note.
pages.en: In an unstable spiral mode the aircraft does not naturally settle down after a small disturbance. Its motion feeds on itself and progressively worsens unless the pilot intervenes. Bank angle is the first giveaway. Instead of stabilising at a constant bank or rolling back toward level, the bank continues to increase. As the bank steepens, the turn radius shrinks and the aircraft follows a tighter, more aggressive spiral path. As that happens, airspeed increases. In a steepening turn the vertical component of lift is reduced, so the aircraft begins to descend; the nose tends to drop and gravity accelerates the aircraft, so speed builds quickly. Higher airspeed makes the situation more demanding, because control inputs become more sensitive, structural limits can be approached, and the g-load during recovery can rise sharply. The pitch attitude is typically nose-low. This nose-down attitude is not the cause by itself, but it reinforces the problem: it increases the descent rate and accelerates the aircraft, which tightens the spiral further and reduces the time available to correct. The inevitable result is rapid altitude loss. Even if the turn initially feels mild, an unstable spiral can consume altitude quickly once the bank and speed start increasing. That is why early recognition matters: stopping the bank and controlling the speed early is far easier than trying to recover once the aircraft is fast, steeply banked and descending hard.

pages.t: Spiral Dive: A Hazardous Descending Turn with Increasing Airspeed and Bank
pages.on: Infographic: characteristics and recognition ("low yaw rate, not a spin"); causes and progression; recovery procedure step by step (reduce power, level wings, gently pull up).
pages.en: A spiral dive is a hazardous descending turn in which both the bank angle and the airspeed keep increasing. It is not a spin. The controls usually remain effective, so it can fool pilots into thinking they can simply pull out — which is exactly what makes it dangerous. How to recognise it: you will see a steep bank that continues to increase, a rapidly rising airspeed, often heading toward the yellow arc, and increasing g-forces as the turn tightens. The descent rate is typically high, but the key cue is that the aircraft is accelerating, not stalling. Spiral dives often happen after a loss of visual reference — for example in cloud, or when the pilot is distracted and fails to notice a small bank developing. Why does it happen? The primary cause is a stability imbalance: strong directional stability with weaker lateral stability. A small, uncorrected bank leads to a turn. In the turn the outer wing moves faster and makes more lift, which can steepen the bank further. As bank increases, the vertical component of lift decreases, so the aircraft begins to descend. As the nose drops, airspeed builds quickly, and without correction the turn tightens and both speed and g-loading can increase dramatically. Recovery is a strict sequence. One: reduce power — bring the throttle back to idle to stop the acceleration and help reduce the g-forces needed for recovery. Two: level the wings — use coordinated aileron and rudder to roll the aircraft back to wings level. This is the priority. Three: gently pull up — only after the wings are level, smoothly raise the nose to recover from the dive. A critical warning: at high airspeed the controls are very sensitive; avoid abrupt pull-ups, because excessive g-forces can overstress the aircraft. The safest mindset is: power back, wings level, then a gentle recovery to level flight.

numbers: Static stability = initial tendency; dynamic stability = motion over time. Want positive static + positive dynamic.
Longitudinal: AoA ↑ → nose-down restoring moment. Static margin = CG to NP distance (% MAC); CG must be forward of the NP.
Forward CG: more stable, heavier forces, higher VS. Aft CG: less stable, lighter forces, poorer stall/spin recovery.
Phugoid: long period (tens of seconds), lightly damped, speed↔height, AoA ≈ constant. Short period: ≈ 1–2 s, heavily damped.
Dutch roll: lateral (dihedral effect) strong vs directional. Spiral instability: directional strong vs lateral.
C172S/T206H: propeller clockwise from the cockpit → left yaw at high power → right rudder.
Spiral dive recovery: POWER idle → WINGS level (coordinated) → gentle PULL. Spiral = airspeed high and rising; spin = low and steady.
C172S ASI (POH — SME): yellow arc 129–163 KIAS, Vne 163 KIAS.
